Mount Kenya is Africa's second-highest peak at seventeen thousand fifty-seven feet, located in central Kenya near the equator. A dramatic glaciated mountain with twin peaks called Batian and Nelion, it presents extensive rock climbing terrain. The final approach to Batian requires technical rock climbing, separated from Nelion by a dramatic snow-filled gap. Kenya is technically more challenging than Kilimanjaro and appeals to mountaineers seeking alpine rock skills in addition to high-altitude endurance. Perpetual glaciers and snow adorn the upper reaches, though glaciers have retreated significantly in recent decades due to climate change. Europeans first summited the peak in eighteen ninety-nine when Halford Mackinder and his party reached the technical summit, though local populations had reached lower altitudes. Climbing Kenya requires rock-climbing skill and experience. The standard Point Lenana route avoids the technical crux and offers views but doesn't summit the true peak. Acclimatization is variable. The mountain's equatorial location and rainfall patterns create unpredictable weather, with climbing season peaking in February and August.
